Jonas,

Thanks again for the demo last week. As part of our security intake for the RFP, the security team has asked for an attestation pack that covers tenant-level segmentation, egress controls, and your mitigation for KV cache/data residency cross-tenant risks. Specifically could you provide:

- A concise playbook that describes isolation boundaries (control plane vs data plane), per-tenant network zones, and failover behavior.
- A network diagram showing tenant routing, sidecars/proxies, and egress filtering points.
- A short threat-model summary that calls out worst-case cross-tenant scenarios and mitigations.
- Evidence artifacts (config snippets, audit log sample, and test run results) if possible.

We need these by EOD Thursday so our InfoSec can include them in the scoring. If there are any required NDAs or paperwork, flag them.

Appreciate it,

Martin Blake
Head of Security Operations
Cedar Capital

Martin / Priya,

Attached are the items requested to start:

- redwood-tenant-seg-playbook-v1.2.pdf (playbook, isolation model, canary & rollback guidance)
- network-diagram-v3.png (annotated zones, sidecar/proxy placement, egress enforcement points)
- threat-model-summary-202705.md (high-level scenarios + mitigations)

High-level summary of what's included:
- Control plane is logically separated; all customer metadata in the control plane is encrypted and access-controlled.
- Data plane uses tenant-specific namespaces and sidecar proxies to enforce egress allowlists and TLS termination.
- KV cache is namespaced per-tenant at the application layer; cache keys include tenant-scoped prefixes and cryptographic tagging to prevent accidental cross-tenant reads.
- Failover: when a node is evicted, KV cache entries are invalidated for the affected tenant; traffic is routed to a fallback model variant to avoid using stale in-memory state.

Next steps/action items:
- Marissa: assembling the evidence bundle (configs, audit-log samples, test reports).
- Kim: security sign-off on the threat-model writeup and any additional controls we should include.

If you want a short call to walk through the diagram and mitigations, I can set one up tomorrow.

Jonas / Marissa —

Thanks for the quick turnaround and the attachments. A couple of follow-ups from our security team after a quick read-through:

1) Sidecar egress allowlists: do you enforce egress at the sidecar itself (host level + proxy) or rely on upstream network ACLs? Which layer is authoritative and how do you prevent a misconfigured host ACL from permitting traffic?

2) KV cache isolation: can you point to the exact mechanism for tenant scoping? The threat-model summary mentions "namespacing + cryptographic tagging" — does that mean you use per-tenant keys, or is it application-level prefixes only?

3) Eviction/failure case: if a node with resident KV entries is removed under high load, what is the maximum window where stale entries could be served? Are there metrics or tests you can share?

4) For our compliance team — any evidence of periodic assertion (e.g., automated tests run daily/weekly) would be helpful.

If it's easier, we can take a 30-minute call with Kim and Marissa to go over the technical points.

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Priya Rao <priya.rao@cedarcap.com>, Martin Blake <m.blake@cedarcap.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas.weber@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Tenant segmentation attestations and diagrams - Cedar Cap RFP follow-up

Priya / Martin —

Thanks for the follow-ups. Short answers with pointers to the artifacts in the attached playbook and evidence bundle below. I'm happy to expand any item or schedule the 30-minute technical deep-dive.

1) Sidecar egress enforcement
- Authoritative enforcement is at the sidecar proxy layer. Sidecars run as unprivileged processes in the same pod/instance and enforce per-tenant egress allowlists via an internal policy agent (policy is stored in the control plane and pushed to sidecars).
- Host-level ACLs (iptables rules) are defense-in-depth. We treat host ACLs as supplementary — if a host ACL is misconfigured, sidecar policy still blocks unauthorized egress because sidecars perform deep packet inspection and application-layer allowlists.
- Evidence: see config/snippets/egress-filter-example.conf (plays out the sidecar policy), and tests/egress-enforcement-run-20270517.md for the verification run.

2) KV cache isolation mechanism
- Primary mechanism: application-level tenant namespacing (cache keys include a tenant ID + versioned namespace).
- Cryptographic tagging is an additional integrity check: each cache entry includes an HMAC over (tenant_id || key || namespace_version) using a per-cluster HMAC key rotated monthly. This prevents accidental cache reads when keys are copied between environments or during migration.
- We do not rely on tenant-specific encryption keys per-customer for low-latency cache entries; instead we combine namespacing + HMAC tagging + mandatory access checks at the cache API layer.
- Evidence: see tests/kv-isolation-run-20270517.md and infra/provisioning-templates.md which show the namespace enforcement.

3) Eviction/failure window and metrics
- On graceful eviction we run an eviction hook that flushes the tenant-specific entries from memory and logs the operation to the audit stream (audit-samples/ingress-egress-audit-202705.csv). For unplanned node loss, the worst-case window is bounded by the TTL applied to in-memory cache entries (default 60s for model-inference caches) and the time-to-detection for the orchestration layer (typically <30s in our monitored fleets).
- In practice, our simulated chaos runs show 95th percentile exposure < 85s; see tests/kv-isolation-run-20270517.md for the test harness and results.

4) Periodic assertions
- We run daily automated regression tests for egress enforcement and weekly chaos runs for eviction scenarios; results are stored in our evidence bucket and summarized in confluence (linked above).
- Attached evidence-bundle-cedar-202705.zip contains the most recent test outputs, audit slices, and config snippets.

Other mitigations called out in the playbook: per-tenant request tagging, transport-level mutual TLS between sidecar and upstream services, and roll-forward/rollback guidance for canarying model variants when we detect anomalous cross-tenant behaviors.

If you'd like, I can publish a short appendix that extracts the exact config lines you can paste into your compliance checklist — happy to do that prior to your deadline.

Regards,
Kimberly Park
Principal Security Engineer, Redwood Inference
kimberly.park@redwood.com
